title: Taking a Greek surplus-food startup abroad: why India said no, and where to go instead
summary: A cross-border expansion project for a Greek startup that sells surprise boxes of leftover food. The founders asked about India; our field research said no, so we built a data-led way to pick the next country.
role: Cross-border expansion strategy and an India-adapted business model

chapters.title: A surprise box of today's leftovers

blocks.markdown:
*A cross-border expansion project for a startup in Greece, 2024. The startup's name is kept private. About 8 minutes to read, plus the full deck.*

A **surplus-food mystery box** is a bag of food that a café, bakery or restaurant could not sell today, sold through an app at a low price. You pay first and collect at closing time. You do not know exactly what is inside, hence the "mystery".

The startup we worked with runs this model in Greece, and it does decently well there. Its founders came to us with one question: **can we take this to India?**

items.title: For the vendor
items.text: Food that would go in the bin earns some money instead. e.g. a bakery recovers part of the cost of the bread left at 9 pm.

items.title: For the customer
items.text: A good meal for much less than the menu price, in exchange for not choosing what is in it.

items.title: Why Greece suits it
items.text: Food rules in Greece are strict, so vendors cannot carry today's food over to sell tomorrow. Thus the leftover has to go somewhere tonight, and the app is that place. Customers also collect the box themselves, so there is no delivery charge to eat into the low price.

items.title: Why expand now
items.text: Competitors already work the same space, so growth at home has a ceiling. Hence the founders were looking abroad.

blocks.heading: A note on the name
blocks.text: The startup is not named in this write-up. Its name and logo are covered on the slides below.

blocks.markdown:
**Field research** is going to the people who will use and supply a product and asking them, instead of guessing from a desk. Before building any model for India, our team did extensive research on the ground: we interviewed food vendors, and spoke to people who use food and deal apps about how they buy.

The answer was clear. The mystery model does not work in India, for three reasons.

**(i) Weak pressure to clear food the same day:** In India the rules do not stop a vendor from selling today's food tomorrow. So the vendor has no deadline, and hence no reason to sell it cheap tonight. e.g. unsold sweets or snacks are often simply on the counter again the next morning. Without that deadline, there is no steady supply of boxes.

**(ii) Too many food needs for one surprise box:** This was the bigger reason. A box only works if almost anyone is happy with almost anything in it. Indian diets split far too finely for that: vegetarian, Jain, non-vegetarian, South Indian, North Indian, and more inside each. e.g. a Jain customer who avoids onion and garlic cannot take a chance on a box that may hold a biryani. Thus the "mystery" that makes the product fun in Greece becomes a risk the customer will not take in India.

**(iii) Indians expect delivery to the door, and the weather backs it:** In Greece the economics work because there is no delivery cost in them: the customer walks in and collects the box. Indian customers are used to food arriving at the doorstep. e.g. Swiggy and Zomato have made a 30-minute delivery the normal way to order. The weather adds to this: in much of India the heat and the rain make walking a long way to collect food hard work for most of the year. So customers would want delivery, and adding delivery would wipe out the low price that makes the box worth buying, hence the model breaks.

We did not stop at "no". To understand why the model works where it does, we went to Greece and **used the startup's app and a competitor's app ourselves**. This showed us the customer experience from ordering to pick-up, and what a market needs for the model to succeed. Those needs became the yardstick for choosing a better country.

For the full India analysis, including the India-fit model we presented and the threat from Swiggy and Zomato, read [Can a surplus-food box work in India?](#case-india-surplus-food-market-entry)

chapters.title: From data points to a country

blocks.markdown: **Country selection** is a way of choosing the next market by scoring each option on the same few facts, instead of on gut feel. Our method had five steps.

steps.phase: Step 1: Learn why it works at home
steps.text: From Greece and the two apps we listed what the model needs: lots of food left over, customers who like a deal, and rules that push vendors to clear food daily.

steps.phase: Step 2: Turn each need into a number
steps.text: Each need became a criterion we could measure the same way for every country. These are the six criteria below.
We compared Germany, Cyprus and the UK, using Greece as the benchmark, on every criterion side by side.
For each country we used the same template: demographics, food waste, rules, campaigns, culture and competitors. Every gap in the data was filled with what it means for our plan.

steps.phase: Step 5: Pick the cheapest good fit
steps.text: We weighed market size against the cost and risk of getting in, and arrived at the most economical choice of country.

blocks.markdown:
### The six criteria

**(i) Food wastage per capita:** The more food is wasted, the more boxes there are to sell, hence the bigger our impact.

**(ii) Income share of the bottom 60%:** Our customers are the middle and lower-middle classes, so we want countries where they hold a fair share of income.

**(iii) Ease of doing business:** How easy it is to register, hire and start operations. A high score means a faster and cheaper launch.

**(iv) Employment ratio:** People in work have less time to cook. e.g. someone leaving the office at 7 pm is more likely to pick up a box on the way home.

**(v) Population aged 15 to 64:** This is the app-using, working-age group we sell to, thus the size of the real market.

**(vi) GDP per capita:** We wanted a middle band. Very rich countries were left out, because people there are less interested in a cheaper end-of-day meal.

blocks.title: The shortlist side by side (figures from our slides)

blocks.markdown:
### What the data told us

**Germany and the UK:** Big markets with high food waste and the easiest places to start a business. But both already have strong competitors, including Too Good To Go, which runs the same model as our startup, plus SIRPLUS and foodsharing in Germany and Olio and Karma in the UK. Hence entry there means paying to win customers from a rival.

**Cyprus:** The smallest market, but the highest food waste per person in Europe in our data (397 kg a year) and about €1,000 of waste per inhabitant. It is close to Greece in culture, economy and distance. e.g. people eat out in meze, many small shared dishes, much like Greek dining. And the competition slide shows no consumer app, only a hotel food-waste research project. Thus a launch there needs little new learning and little marketing spend.

blocks.heading: Our recommendation: Cyprus
blocks.text: We recommended Cyprus first. Germany and the UK are bigger prizes, but winning there means outspending established rivals. Cyprus fitted the founders' budget (which stays confidential), needed the least change to the model, and had no direct competitor. We also presented an India-fit version of the model, but it made more economical sense to grow in Cyprus before taking on a market as big as India. Hence Cyprus was our final recommendation.

chapters.title: A deck built to suit a young, playful startup

blocks.markdown: A **storyboard** is the plan of a presentation before any slide is made: one line for what each slide must prove, in the order the audience needs to hear it. I wrote the content and designed the deck myself, and shaped it to fit the startup's culture. AI played a small, specific part.

**(i) Start from the client's culture:** The startup is young and informal, and its product is a fun surprise. So the deck had to feel the same: light, visual and quick to read, not a dense consulting report. e.g. every criterion and every section header carries an icon, so a founder can follow the story by skimming.

**(ii) One question per slide:** Each slide answers one question, such as "how big is the market?" or "who is already there?". This keeps the story moving from criteria, to comparison, to each country.

**(iii) The same template for every country:** Cyprus, Germany and the UK each get the same set of slides: profile and food waste, rules and campaigns, culture, and competitors. Thus the founders can compare countries slide for slide.

**(iv) AI for images and polish only:** We used AI for two jobs: making the images, and making long content crisp. e.g. a dense paragraph on food regulations was cut down to a few short lines a founder can read at a glance. The research, the storyline and the design were our own, hence the deck says what we found, just more clearly.
Here is the full deck as we presented it, one slide at a time. The startup's name and logo are covered.
